desc:
A park has n junctions labelled 1 to n, and two visitors, Alice and Bob. Every path joins two junctions in both directions and has a type: edges[i] = [type, a, b].

  • type 1: only Alice may walk it,
  • type 2: only Bob may walk it,
  • type 3: both may walk it.

You may close down (delete) some paths, but afterwards each visitor must still be able to reach every junction from every other junction using the paths they are allowed to use. Return the maximum number of paths you can delete, or -1 if this is impossible even without deleting anything.

n = 4, edges = [[3,1,2],[3,2,3],[1,1,3],[1,2,4],[1,1,2],[2,3,4]]

result = 2     (delete [1,1,3] and [1,1,2])
constraints: type is 1, 2 or 3; 1 ≤ a, b ≤ n and a ≠ b
The same type is never listed twice for the same pair of junctions (different types between one pair are allowed)
hints: Each visitor needs a spanning tree of the junctions made of paths they may use, so each needs exactly n - 1 paths at least. Shared paths (type 3) can serve both at once.
Prefer shared paths. First process all type-3 paths: keep one only if it joins two different groups (of a union-find that is used for both visitors).

Then process type 1 with Alice's own union-find and type 2 with Bob's, keeping a path only when it merges two groups. At the end each visitor must have exactly one group, otherwise the answer is -1. The answer is the total number of paths minus the paths kept.
editorial: A set of paths works for Alice exactly when her allowed paths (types 1 and 3) connect all junctions, and likewise for Bob (types 2 and 3). Minimal such sets are spanning trees, so we want to keep as few paths as possible. A shared path counts for both visitors, so it is never worse than a private path for the same pair: use shared paths first.

Keep two union-find structures, one for Alice and one for Bob. Pass 1: for every type-3 path, try to merge in Alice's structure; if it merged (that means it also merges in Bob's, since the two structures are identical during this pass), merge in Bob's too and count one kept path. Pass 2: type-1 paths go through Alice's structure only, type-2 paths through Bob's, each counted when it merges two groups. Finally both structures must be a single group, else return -1; otherwise the answer is len(edges) - kept.

Why greedy is right: shared paths first give both trees a common backbone, and every other kept path is needed by exactly one visitor. Any valid solution has at least as many kept paths. Time O(m · α(n)).
